notes.text: Peter answered the people — Who were running together, and inquiring into the circumstances of the fact.

The God of our fathers — This was wisely introduced in the beginning of his discourse, that it might appear they taught no new religion, inconsistent with that of Moses, and were far from having the least design to divert their regards from the God of Israel. Hath glorified his Son - By this miracle, whom ye delivered up - When God had given him to you, and when ye ought to have received him as a most precious treasure, and to have preserved him with all your power.
Ye renounced the Holy One — Whom God had marked out as such; and the Just One - Even in the judgment of Pilate.
His name — Himself: his power and love. The faith which is by him - Of which he is the giver, as well as the object.

And now, brethren -- a word full of courtesy and compassion, I know — He speaks to their heart, that through ignorance ye did it - which lessened, though it could not take away, the guilt. As did also your rulers - The prejudice lying from the authority of the chief priests and elders, he here removes, but with great tenderness. He does not call them our, but your rulers. For as the Jewish dispensation ceased at the death of Christ, consequently so did the authority of its rulers.
But God — Who was not ignorant, permitted this which he had foretold, to bring good out of it.

Be converted — Be turned from sin and Satan unto God. See chap. xxvi, 20. But this term, so common in modern writings, very rarely occurs in Scripture: perhaps not once in the sense we now use it, for an entire change from vice to holiness. That the times of refreshing - Wherein God largely bestows his refreshing grace, may come - To you also. To others they will assuredly come, whether ye repent or no.

glossa.text: *The God of Abraham,* etc. ((RAB.)) Three are commemorated, with no ungodly man coming between, either on account of the primacy of justice, or, etc., *as far as* which also is likewise observed in the spiritual generation.
*You killed,* by will and by word, and this against the law, which says: He that shall kill a man willingly, he also shall be killed.
*Perfect soundness.* In the two things which have been foretold.
*Through ignorance.* Two things wrought together: your ignorance, and the foreknowledge of God.
*By the mouth of all,* etc. Therefore was it necessary that it should be fulfilled, because not one, but all had prophesied.
*That sins may be blotted out.* Then shall sins be fully blotted out, when by the power of the resurrection death shall be destroyed last.

notes.text: O God — The witness and defender of my righteous cause.

My glory — By his glory probably he means that honour which God had conferred upon him. Vanity - Wickedness. Lying - Those calumnies which they raised against him, to make him odious to all the people.

Godly — Me, whom, though you traduce as an hypocrite, God hath pronounced to be a man after his own heart, 1 Sam. xiii, 14. For himself - In his stead, or to be his vicegerent, as all kings are, and especially the kings of God's own people.

In awe — Be afraid, if not of me, yet of God, who hath engaged in my cause. Sin not - By prosecuting your rebellion against God's authority. On your bed - Calmly consider these things in the silent night, when you are at leisure from distracting business. Be still - Compose your tumultuous minds.

Offer — Unto God, that he may be reconciled to you. Righteousness - Righteous sacrifices; which requires that the persons offering them be righteous and do righteous things, and offer them with an honest mind, with faith and true repentance. Without which, he intimates, that all their sacrifices were of no esteem with God, and would be wholly unprofitable to them.

Many — Of my followers, who are weary of waiting upon God. Who - Who will put an end to our troubles, and give us tranquility. Lift up - Upon me and my friends. Give us an assurance of thy love, and evidence it by thy powerful assistance.

Thou hast — Whatsoever thou shalt do with me for the future, I have at present unspeakable satisfaction in the testimonies of thy love to my soul; more than worldly persons have in the time of a plentiful harvest.

In peace — In tranquility of mind, resting securely upon God's promises. David beseeches God to hear his prayer, ver. 1-3. Assures himself of God's justice against his enemies, ver. 4-6. Declares his resolution: to serve God, ver. 7. Prays for himself and the people of God, and against his enemies, ver. 8-12. To the chief musician upon Nehiloth, A psalm of David. Title of the psalm. Nehiloth - This is no where else used in scripture. It is thought to signify a wind-instrument, as Neginoth signified stringed instruments.

glossa.text: « When I called upon, etc. » ((CASS.)) By his own example he rebukes the unbelieving concerning false things. « Thou hast enlarged for me. » ((Ibid.)) From the straits of sadness thou hast led me into the breadth of joy. V. « We rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation, etc. » ((Rom. V.)) He first showed that he had been heard: now, as though having God in his heart, he speaks to him. « Have mercy on me. » He had mercy concerning righteousness and concerning the enlarging. Again, have mercy against the miseries of this life. « My prayer. » Concerning the good things that are to be asked for. And when it is thus concerning me, « Ye sons of men, how long will ye be heavy of heart? »
« Ye love vanity, etc. » ((CASS.)) With your desire you embrace, with labour you seek vain idols, and lies, which are not God: or earthly things, which do not do what they promise.

« And know ye, etc. » The new man being set forth, he bids them put off the old. ((AUG.)) Note that « And » is placed at beginnings, so that it may join the things said with the vision that is in the heart, so here, as: « Love not vain things. And know ye. » But the diapsalma forbids their being so joined. Diapsalma, according to Jerome, is always, the Hebrews, Sela, that is, always, in confirmation of the preceding part. Sympsalma, that is, the joining of a psalm. « The Lord will hear. » Concerning rest it is thus, and so with you: and therefore cry out, being thus worthy to be heard.

« Be ye angry. » If a motion of the soul arises which is not in our power, let not reason consent to it. ((CASS.)) A motion of the soul is not in our power, but by the grace of God we are able to temper it: what therefore belongs to custom, he permits; what belongs to fault, he forbids.

((HIER.)) This the Apostle teaches: « Let not the sun go down upon your anger ((Ephes. IV)), » so that it is altogether a sin to be angry even lightly: but it is righteousness to soften anger by a swift repentance. « In your hearts. » ((AUG.)) Concerning those things which you handle in the heart, which God knows: that is, concerning consent; and concerning those things which you turn over in the bed, that is, in the delight of the flesh, in which reason dwells captive, as a wild beast in its lair, « Be ye pricked, » through penance; or the beds are the thoughts of the fierce. ((CASS.)) Venial is the anger which is not carried through to effect. Diapsalma. « Sacrifice ye. » ((CASS.)) The old man being laid aside, we are bidden to be offered in sacrifice, because we are sure of good things. ((AUG.)) « The sacrifice of righteousness, » a contrite spirit, that, punishing itself, it may be slain to God: or, just works after penance, which the diapsalma marks, that from the old life there may be a passing over to the new, and so hope ye for good things. But because there is scarcely one who loves the inner goods, he adds:
« Many say: Who showeth us good things? » Things to come, namely, of which they doubt and despair. Answering to which he shows briefly what good things are to be sought.

« The light is signed upon us, etc. » ((AUG.)) This light is the whole and the true good of man, wherewith he is signed, as a penny with the image of the king. « Light. » ((AUG.)) Light, that is, a shining countenance, and one that enlightens us, an image whereby thou art known. ((CASS.)) Or: the cross has been imprinted upon us, for a sign of our king, which is the light of the countenance: because in such men God shines out. The image of creation is reason; of re-creation, grace; of likeness, the whole Trinity. « In the heart. ((AUG.)) Not without in vain things, but within, where God dwells, is gladness to be sought.
« From the fruit. » ((CAS.)) Because they think that in these things the good is consummated. These three, as being more suited to human uses, he sets down for all riches.

« In peace in the selfsame. » ((CASS.)) But I will sleep in the peace of the mind, here forgetful of the world, and I will rest in the time to come: because I am already in one hope, not in the manifoldness of the world. « In peace I will sleep and I will rest. » ((AUG.)) From all the things of the world, when this mortal shall put on immortality: and this will truly be, because it is already hope: and this is: « For thou, O Lord, » and assuredly that will be which is hoped for.

notes.text: That we should be called — That is, should be, the children of God. Therefore the world knoweth us not - They know not what to make of us. We are a mystery to them.

It doth not yet appear — Even to ourselves. What we shall be - It is something ineffable, which will raise the children of God to be, in a manner, as God himself. But we know, in general, that when he, the Son of God, shall appear, we shall be like him - The glory of God penetrating our inmost substance. For we shall see him as he is - Manifestly, without a veil. And that sight will transform us into the same likeness.
And every one that hath this hope in him — In God.
Whosoever committeth sin — Thereby transgresseth the holy, just, and good law of God, and so sets his authority at nought; for this is implied in the very nature of sin.

And ye know that he — Christ. Was manifested - That he came into the world for this very purpose. To take away our sins - To destroy them all, root and branch, and leave none remaining. And in him is no sin - So that he could not suffer on his own account, but to make us as himself.

Whosoever abideth in communion with him, by loving faith, sinneth not — While he so abideth. Whosoever sinneth certainly seeth him not - The loving eye of his soul is not then fixed upon God; neither doth he then experimentally know him - Whatever he did in time past.
Let no one deceive you — Let none persuade you that any man is righteous but he that uniformly practices righteousness; he alone is righteous, after the example of his Lord.

glossa.text: *See,* etc. Consider diligently with how great and what manner of gifts God has shown his fatherly charity toward us. For he granted that in this world we should be named sons of God in name and in deed, and that in the world to come we should be so, by possessing the inherited blessedness. *He gave.* To this end God gave charity, that we might know how to love him and be able to, yet not as servants a master, but as sons a father. Whence it is said: *And as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God ((Joan. I))*.

*We are the sons of God.* As if he should say: To be and to be called sons of God, what dignity is that? he answers: *Dearly beloved, now we are the sons of God.* Now through the miracles which we do and through purity of life it appears that we are sons of God, but whatever is in the present is little in comparison with what is to come. *We shall be like to him.* For when we shall fully enjoy the contemplation of the unchangeable and eternal Godhead, we also shall be immortal and eternal in him: not indeed the same as he, but like, because we are a creature and were made to his likeness. *Because we shall see.* According as the Word was made flesh, the wicked have seen him, and in the judgment they shall see him: but how the Word in the beginning was with the Father, the just alone shall see: the wicked man shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.
*He sanctifieth himself. ((BEDA.))* He does not take away free will, when he says, etc., *as far as* saying to God: *Thou art my helper, forsake me not ((Psal. XXVI))*.
*And sin,* etc. ((ID.)) What the Latins call law, the Greeks, etc., *as far as* they who corrupt the innocence of the natural law are guilty of transgression.

*And you know.* Lest we (who cannot be free of sins and iniquities ) should despair of salvation, he adds that through Christ we are loosed from sins. Not only therefore have we been made sons of God through grace, and do we hope that we shall be like to him, but we are also freed from iniquity: because for this reason *he appeared, that he might take away sins,* from which iniquity let no one excuse himself.

*He that sinneth hath not seen him.* And he that abideth in him sinneth not. And in this *let no man deceive you,* by saying either that justice is from man, or that anyone can abide in God together with sin, because all justice is from God, and all sin is from the devil.

*He that doth justice.* That is: he who has the act of justice and the intention is indeed just, but not of himself: but as that one is, he proceeds from the same root. Justice is in that one principally, in this one secondarily, in that one naturally, in this one by adoption. This very thing, that he who is just is just from him.

notes.text: Jesus stood in the midst of them — It was just as easy to his Divine power to open a door undiscernibly, as it was to come in at a door opened by some other hand. Mark xvi, 14, 19; John xx, 19.
He showed them his hands and his feet — That they might either see or feel the prints of the nails.
While they believed not for joy — They did in some sense believe: otherwise they would not have rejoiced. But their excess of joy prevented a clear, rational belief.
He took it and ate before them — Not that he had any need of food; but to give them still further evidence.

And he said — On the day of his ascension. In the law, and the prophets, and the Psalms - The prophecies as well as types, relating to the Messiah, are contained either in the books of Moses (usually called the law) in the Psalms, or in the writings of the prophets; little being said directly concerning him in the historical books.

Then opened he their understanding, to understand the Scriptures — He had explained them before to the two as they went to Emmaus. But still they understood them not, till he took off the veil from their hearts, by the illumination of his Spirit.

Beginning at Jerusalem — This was appointed most graciously and wisely: graciously, as it encouraged the, greatest sinners to repent, when they saw that even the murderers of Christ were not excepted from mercy: and wisely, as hereby Christianity was more abundantly attested; the facts being published first on the very spot where they happened.

glossa.text: *Jesus stood,* etc. This appearance is that of which John says ((Joan. XX)): *When it was late that day,* etc., *and he said to them: Peace be to you.* But as to John's saying that Thomas was not with them, while Luke says that these two found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, it is to be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to them as they spoke of these things.

*To see a spirit. And he said to them.* The disciples had known him to be true man, but after he died they do not believe that true flesh could rise from the sepulchre on the third day. They think therefore that they see the spirit which he sent forth in the passion; but the Lord takes away this error.

*Why are you troubled. ((AMBR.))* The apostles believed, but nevertheless they are troubled, etc., *as far as* that the Lord, with the doors shut, poured himself in unforeseen with his body.

*Thoughts,* etc. False ones, not descending from above, but rising up in the heart like an evil weed. I require the faith which I planted in you; what has sprung from yourselves I condemn. If there is no truth of the resurrection, the fruit of the passion is lost.

*Handle and see.* By many proofs he persuades them of the resurrection, offering himself both to be seen by their eyes and to be handled by their hands; and while by their handling he shows bones and flesh, he marks the state of his own resurrection and of ours, in which our body will be both subtle through the effect of a spiritual power, and palpable through the truth of its nature. After the resurrection the Lord showed in his body two contrary things: both what is palpable, of the same nature, that he might form them to faith, and what is incorruptible, of another glory, that he might invite them to the reward.

*He showed them his hands,* etc. That by showing the scar of his wounds he might heal the wound of unbelief; which scars he both kept then and will keep in the judgment. First, to establish faith in the resurrection; then, that, entreating the Father for us, he may always show what kind of death he endured for man; thirdly, that he may intimate to those redeemed by his death how mercifully they have been helped, by setting before them the tokens of that same death. But lastly, that in the judgment he may declare how justly the impious are condemned, by showing the scar which he received from them. Not therefore from any inability to heal them did he keep the scars, but that he might carry about the perpetual triumph of his victory.

*Have you here anything.* To convey the truth of the resurrection, he willed not only to be touched but to eat with them; not that either he or we after the resurrection ought to need food, but that he might make manifest that he was a body, not a spirit; he ate by power, not by necessity. In one way the thirsting earth soaks up water, in another the hot ray of the sun: the former by need, the latter by power.

*Of a broiled fish.* The broiled fish is the Mediator himself who suffered, taken in the waters of the human race by the snare of death, broiled at the time of the passion. He is also to us a honeycomb in the resurrection. The honeycomb in the wax, that is, the Godhead in the manhood. In the eating of this honey it is signified that he receives into his body, unto eternal rest, those who, when they feel tribulations for God, do not withdraw from the love of the inward sweetness. They who are broiled here shall there be filled with the true sweetness.

*And when he had eaten.* He takes away all evasions : he was seen, he was touched, he ate; and lest in anything he should seem to have deluded the human senses, he puts his hands to the Scriptures, so that even if it should seem, as the pagans say, that by magic arts he was able to do what he willed, they may at least see that he could not have prophesied before he was born.

*Then he opened.* After the sight, after the touch, after the law recalled to mind, he opened their understanding, that they might understand what they see and read; then, after the truth of his own body had been commended, he commends the unity of the Church: *And that there should be preached in his name.*

*It behoved,* etc. It behoved that the ministers who were to preach penance and remission unto all nations should begin from Jerusalem. Not only because to them were entrusted the oracles of God, and because theirs is the adoption of sons, and the glory the testaments, and the law-giving; but for this reason also, that the Gentiles, entangled in various errors and crimes, might by this token above all of the divine loving-kindness be roused to the hope of pardon: that he grants pardon to those who crucified the Son of God.

echoes.text: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
echoes.note: 'The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers' (v. 13) reproduces the patriarchal covenant formula of the burning bush, anchoring the resurrection proclamation in the God who self-identifies to Moses.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'has glorified his Servant (pais) Jesus' (v. 13) echoes the LXX of the fourth Servant Song, 'my servant... shall be exalted and glorified'; the combination of pais + glorification is a deliberate Servant identification.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: The expanded title 'the God of our fathers' as the LORD's memorial name reinforces the Exodus 3 self-disclosure; v. 15 supplies the 'God of your fathers... my name for ever' phrasing behind Peter's formula.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: The 'Righteous One' (v. 14) whom they denied draws on the suffering Servant who is called 'the righteous one, my servant' who justifies many; coheres with the pais/Servant frame of v. 13.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'the Holy One' (v. 14) recalls the Davidic 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' cited fully in Acts 2:27; the title clusters here with the resurrection claim 'God raised from the dead' (v. 15).

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'whom you delivered up' (v. 13) faintly mirrors the Servant who 'was delivered up' (paredothe) for the transgressors; the handing-over language belongs to the same Servant matrix.

echoes.text: “‘When you shall err, and not observe all these commandments, which Yahweh has spoken to Moses, even all that Yahweh has commanded you by Moses, from the day that Yahweh gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations; then it shall be, if it was done unwittingly, without the knowledge of the congregation, that all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering, for a pleasant aroma to Yahweh, with its meal offering, and its […]
echoes.note: 'you did this in ignorance' (v. 17) invokes the Torah distinction between unwitting sin (atonable) and high-handed sin; Peter casts the crucifixion as forgivable ignorance, opening the call to repentance.

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'that your sins may be blotted out' (v. 19) echoes the LORD's promise 'I am he that blotteth out thy transgressions'; the blotting-out image of divine forgiveness is distinctive.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: 'times of restoration (apokatastasis) of all things' (v. 21) draws on the Elijah-tradition of restoring/turning hearts before the day of the LORD; LXX Mal 3:23-24 uses apokatastesei, the verbal root behind Peter's eschatological 'restoration'.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘If anyone sins unintentionally, in any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and does any one of them:
echoes.note: The priestly category of sinning 'through ignorance' underlies Peter's exoneration in v. 17; thematic, no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.
echoes.note: 'blot out my transgressions' supplies the same penitential idiom behind v. 19; coheres with the call to repent, though Isa 43 is the closer match.

echoes.text: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the great locust, the grasshopper, and the caterpillar, my great army, which I sent among you.
echoes.note: Joel's promise of God restoring the years coheres with the 'times of refreshing... restoration of all things' (vv. 19-21); thematic restoration motif, no verbal link.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Nazareth
places.id: Modern en-Nasira / Nazareth in Lower Galilee, c. 30 km west of the Sea of Galilee. A village of perhaps 200-400 in the early first century, identified through continuous habitation, tomb evidence, and the third-century Caesarea inscription naming it as a priestly course settlement.

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: Israel addressed as 'children of the LORD your God' grounds John's astonishment that believers 'should be called children of God.' The divine-sonship status, once Israel's covenant identity, is here extended to the community. John intensifies the relation with the language of bestowed love.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: Hosea promises that those who were 'not my people' will be called 'children of the living God,' the precise idiom of being 'called children of God.' This eschatological renaming of the people supplies John's vocabulary for present sonship. The passage was a standard locus for adoption-into-sonship.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: God tells Moses no one may see his face and live, the canonical statement of the unseen God. John's hope that 'we will see him just as he is' deliberately reverses this prohibition as eschatological promise. The tension between present hiddenness and future sight is structured by this Exodus limit.

echoes.text: As for me, I shall see your face in righteousness. I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form.
echoes.note: The psalmist hopes to 'behold your face in righteousness' and be 'satisfied with your likeness' upon awaking, the classic beatific-vision text and a likeness motif. John's 'we will be like him, for we will see him' closely mirrors this seeing-and-likeness pairing. The awaking imagery resonates with eschatological revelation.

echoes.text: I will tell the north, ‘Give them up!’ and tell the south, ‘Don’t hold them back! Bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth—
echoes.note: God commands the gathering of 'my sons' and 'my daughters' from the ends of the earth, framing the people as God's children. The verse reinforces the sonship motif John applies to believers. Faint but congruent with the divine-family theme.

echoes.text: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God, Whom I, even I, shall see on my side. My eyes shall see, and not as a stranger. “My heart is consumed within me.
echoes.note: Job hopes that after his skin is destroyed he will 'see God' with his own eyes, an early witness to seeing God beyond death. This undergirds John's confidence that the not-yet-revealed future includes seeing him. The contested textual history of the verse makes the echo suggestive rather than certain.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: Moses uniquely beholds the form/likeness of the LORD, an exceptional clear sight of God amid general hiddenness. John universalizes such direct vision as the believers' destiny. A faint background to seeing him 'as he is.'

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: The Servant 'had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth,' the sinless one who bears others' iniquity. John's 'in him is no sin' and 'he was revealed to take away our sins' draws on the Servant who removes sin while being himself without it. The pairing of sin-bearing and sinlessness is distinctively Isaianic.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: The Servant bears and carries away the sins of the many, the conceptual ground for 'he was revealed to take away our sins.' John's atonement language echoes this vicarious sin-removal. A strong thematic, looser verbal, link.

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.
echoes.note: The penitential confession of transgression and the plea to blot out lawlessness frame sin as 'lawlessness' (anomia in the Greek tradition). John's definition 'sin is lawlessness' draws on this Septuagintal vocabulary. Faint lexical resonance rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The serpent who sins/deceives 'from the beginning' stands behind 'the devil has been sinning from the beginning.' The promised crushing of the serpent's head undergirds the Son's appearing 'to destroy the works of the devil.' This is the foundational devil-as-deceiver-from-the-start text.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: The enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed, with the seed who crushes the serpent, frames both 'destroy the works of the devil' and the children-of-God versus children-of-the-devil opposition. The 'seed' language in 3:9 ('his seed remains in him') plays on this protoevangelium. A primary structural source for the whole pericope.

echoes.text: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: 'Through the devil's envy death entered the world,' an early identification of the Genesis serpent with the devil. This deuterocanonical reading directly supports John's claim that 'he who sins is of the devil.' It bridges Genesis 3 to John's explicit devil terminology.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: The creation refrain of plants bearing seed 'according to its kind' may color the image of God's 'seed' remaining and producing offspring true to their origin. The begetting/seed motif of 3:9 has a creational backdrop. Faint and contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: All these days I appeared to you. I didn’t eat or drink, but you all saw a vision.
echoes.note: Raphael's disclosure, 'I appeared to you, but I did not eat or drink; it was a vision that you saw,' frames the Second-Temple assumption that angelic/spirit visitants only seem to eat. Luke counters precisely this by having the risen Jesus eat real food to prove he is 'not a spirit' but has flesh and bones, engaging Tobit's category. Coherence and availability are strong.

echoes.text: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
echoes.note: Jesus eating broiled fish before them to prove corporeal reality parallels the angels who 'ate' before Abraham at Mamre, the locus classicus for heavenly visitors sharing human food. Luke uses the eating motif as physical proof against the disciples' supposition of a spirit. Recurrence of the 'divine visitor eats' type supports it.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them.
echoes.note: The disciples suppose they see a disembodied 'spirit' (pneuma), reflecting a current view that the righteous dead exist as souls 'in the hand of God.' Luke's insistence on flesh and bones engages and corrects such a discarnate-soul expectation. Conceptual and faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God,
echoes.note: 'In my flesh I shall see God' anticipates an embodied vindication beyond death that resonates with Luke's emphasis on the risen Jesus' flesh and bones. As a faint OT witness to bodily hope it may color the scene, but there is no verbal contact. Contested, low.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' is the programmatic text behind 'repentance and remission of sins... to all the nations.' Luke quotes Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes to it at Acts 1:8, making it the key prophetic warrant for the worldwide mission launched here. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I send out the promise of my Father on you... until you are clothed with power from on high' anticipates Joel's outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, which Luke fulfills explicitly at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel). The Spirit as the Father's promise is the bridge from Luke 24 to Acts. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.
echoes.note: That repentance and forgiveness be proclaimed 'to all the nations' fulfills the Psalter's vision that 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD,' part of the Writings (psalmoi) Jesus names as bearing witness to him. Luke roots the universal mission in the Psalms he has just cited. Coherence with the tripartite-canon statement supports it.

echoes.text: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'Beginning at Jerusalem' enacts the eschatological pattern whereby 'out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem,' the nations streaming to and the word streaming from Zion. Luke reverses the centripetal pilgrimage into a centrifugal mission from Jerusalem. Coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Many nations will go and say, “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law will go out of Zion, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem;
echoes.note: Micah's parallel oracle that 'the word of the LORD' goes forth 'from Jerusalem' to instruct the nations reinforces the Jerusalem-origin of the universal proclamation. The doubled prophetic witness (with Isa 2:3) strengthens the case that Luke draws on the Zion-mission tradition. Recurrence supports medium.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The herald who proclaims good news of salvation from Zion underlies Luke's commissioning of witnesses to preach forgiveness beginning at Jerusalem. Luke's vocabulary of proclaiming (kēryssō) good news echoes the Isaianic herald, a text central to his mission theology. Coherence good.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved... in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape' underwrites repentance/forgiveness proclaimed 'in his name' beginning from Jerusalem. Luke cites Joel 2 at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), making it a strong intertext for the commission. Recurrence in Luke-Acts supports it.

echoes.text: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.
echoes.note: 'Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high' supplies the very phrase 'power from on high' (ex hypsous) for the promised Spirit-endowment. Luke's 'clothed with power from on high' draws on this Isaianic image of the Spirit poured out to renew. Verbal contact ('from on high') gives medium-strong confidence.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your descendants' reinforces the promised-Spirit theme of being clothed with power, an OT pattern of the Spirit poured out as gift and blessing. Together with Joel and Isa 32 it forms the cluster behind the Father's promise. Recurrence within the cluster supports it.

echoes.text: When Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, saying, “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.
echoes.note: 'All things written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms... must be fulfilled' names the threefold Hebrew canon (Torah, Prophets, Writings), and the Law of Moses as a written witness placed beside the ark to testify is the Torah pole of that witness. Luke frames the whole of Scripture, beginning with Moses' written law, as testifying to Christ. Coherence with the canon formula supports it.

echoes.text: But the Spirit of Yahweh came on Gideon; and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together after him.
echoes.note: 'Clothed with power' (enedysasthe) recalls the idiom that the Spirit of the LORD 'clothed itself with' Gideon, the standard OT metaphor for divine empowerment of a chosen agent. Luke's clothing-with-power language may draw on this Spirit-clothing idiom. Faint verbal idiom, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The prologue to Sirach repeatedly names 'the Law and the Prophets and the others/the rest of the books,' the earliest explicit witness to the tripartite division of Hebrew Scripture that Luke 24:44 presupposes ('law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms'). It supplies the Second-Temple canonical framework, not a content-quotation. Availability and coherence support medium.

registers.label: Spare
lines: While we were talking, he stood among us.
Peace be with you, he said.
We were startled, thinking we saw a ghost.
But look at my hands; touch me and see.
He took a piece of fish and ate before us.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He opened our minds to understand. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come and stand close, you who are startled and slow to believe, you who half expect a ghost.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
See his hands, see his feet; this is no spirit but flesh and bone, the friend you watched them kill.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Watch him take the broiled fish and eat it in front of you, ordinary as any supper.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Then he opens your mind like a book, and the light of his face falls on you, and you can lie down in peace.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: He stands among us: do not be afraid.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Touch my hands and feet; it is myself.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He eats the fish and opens up the Scriptures.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us worship in the light of his face.
We are witnesses. Alleluia!
